# Disability Language Style Guide
## Able-bodied
### Autism/autism spectrum disorder/autistic
Opinions vary on how to refer to someone with autism. Some people with autism prefer being referred to as “autistic” or an “autistic person.” Others object to using autistic as an adjective.
[The Autism Self Advocacy Network details this debate](http://autisticadvocacy.org/about-asan/identity-first-language/) .
**NCDJ Recommendation:** Refer to someone as having autistic spectrum disorder only if the information is relevant to the story and if you are confident there is a medical diagnosis. Ask individuals how they prefer to be described.
Many prefer to be described as “autistic,” while others prefer “an autistic person” or a “person with autism.”
**AP style:** The stylebook states that it’s acceptable to use the word “autism” as “an umbrella term for a group of developmental disorders.” It also says it is acceptable to use the word autism in stories. It does not address the use of autistic as an adjective.

sources.title: A Disability Language Style Guide – Franklin County Public Health
sources.excerpt:
# A Disability Language Style Guide
## Consider helpful resources:
### 3. ******Avoid descriptions that imply pity****** .
Disability does not equal suffering! Terms like “afflicted with,” “suffers from” or “victim of” carry the assumption that a person with a disability has a reduced quality of life. Use neutral language when describing a person who has a disability, simply stating the facts.

...

### 6. ******Identity-first language vs. people-first language****** .
For example, “Down syndrome girl” or “autistic boy.” An example of **people-first** language is “a girl with Down syndrome” or “a boy with autism.” Regarding most disabilities, people-first language is preferred.
In some cases—most notably in the Deaf community and among autistic people—identity-first language is preferred. It’s best to ask the person with the disability how they would like to be described.

### 7. Describing people without disabilities.
“Non-disabled” refers to someone who does not have a disability. According to the [University of Kansas Research & Training Center on Independent Living](http://rtcil.org/products/media/guidelines) , non-disabled is the preferred term when comparing people with and without disabilities.

# How to Diversify Autism Representation in the Media and Why Intersectionality Matters
## HIGHLIGHTS
While most autistic characters are portrayed as white male geniuses (like _Rain Man_ and _The Good Doctor_ ), the fact is, autism is exponentially more complex and diverse than what we see on-screen.
In fact, a [study done in 2018 on media portrayals of ASD](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0165178117304225) found that around 46% of the autistic characters on-screen had [savant abilities](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC2677584/) , yet only 10% of autistic people possess these skills in real

...

### Connections with Gender and Sexuality
Although there are many women and LGBTQ+ individuals on the autistic spectrum, in the rare instances where autistic relationships appear on-screen, [they are almost always shown from the male, heterosexual perspective](https://cjds.uwaterloo.ca/index.php/cjds/article/view/428/673) .

must_do.rule: Give the autistic character agency, a drive, and a strong moral compass.
Highlight the character's strengths, such as reading patterns others miss, to reflect a nuanced and positive portrayal.
Center the story and experiences around the autistic character rather than treating them as a secondary plot device.
Ensure the character diversifies media representation by portraying an autistic girl rather than defaulting to the male genius stereotype.

must_not_do.rule: Do not portray the autistic character as a burden to her family or friends.
Do not use non-human othering descriptions in action lines, such as comparing the character's behavior to a robot.
Do not describe the character using language that implies pity, suffering, or a reduced quality of life regarding her autism.
Do not portray the character as having unrealistic savant abilities; focus instead on relatable strengths.
